definition: Application Programming Interface. A way for one program to ask another program for data or actions.
example: The weather app calls an API to get today's forecast.

definition: Software Development Kit. A bundle of tools and code that helps developers build software for a specific platform.
example: The payment company provides an SDK so you can add checkout to your app.

definition: Representational State Transfer. A common style for building web APIs that use ordinary web addresses and requests.
example: The service offers a REST API for reading customer records.

definition: JavaScript Object Notation. A simple text format for storing and sending data as labeled values.
example: The server replied with a JSON file containing the user's name and email.

definition: Command-Line Interface. A way to control a program by typing commands instead of clicking.
example: You can install the tool with one command in the CLI.

definition: Integrated Development Environment. An app where developers write, run and fix code in one place.
example: Most developers write code in an IDE such as VS Code.

definition: A specific web address where an API receives requests.
example: Send the request to the login endpoint.

definition: The main data sent in a request or response, not counting the extra labels around it.
example: The payload contains the new user's name and email.

definition: An error that happens while a program is running and stops it from continuing normally.
example: The app threw an exception when the file was missing.

definition: A list of the steps a program took right before it crashed, used to find the cause.
example: The stack trace shows the crash started in the login function.

definition: To reorganize code so it is cleaner without changing what it does.
example: We will refactor the billing code to make it easier to read.

definition: Code written by someone else that your program needs in order to work.
example: Update the dependency to fix the bug.

definition: Still works for now, but is outdated and will be removed in the future.
example: This feature is deprecated, so use the new one instead.

definition: Safe to repeat: doing it many times gives the same result as doing it once.
example: Deleting a file by name is idempotent, because the second delete changes nothing.

definition: The time when a program is running, or the software that runs it.
example: The error only appears at runtime.

definition: A folder where a project's code and its change history are stored.
example: Push your changes to the repository.

definition: A cap on how many requests you can send to a service in a set time.
example: You hit the rate limit after 100 requests in a minute.

definition: Blocked for a while because too many requests were sent too quickly.
example: The server rate-limited our app after a burst of requests.

definition: Waiting longer after each failed try before trying again, for example 1 second, then 2, then 4.
example: Use exponential backoff so you don't overload the server.

definition: A small random delay added to retries so many clients do not retry at the exact same moment.
example: Add jitter to spread out the retries.

definition: Extra information sent along with a web request or response, such as who you are or what format you want.
example: The Authorization header carries your access token.

definition: Code that sits between two parts of a system and handles shared tasks like checking logins.
example: The middleware checks every request for a valid login.

definition: A bug where something that used to work stops working after a change.
example: The update caused a regression in the search feature.

definition: A programming mistake where code tries to use something that does not exist.
example: The crash was caused by a null pointer.

definition: Domain Name System. The internet's phone book that turns website names into numeric addresses.
example: A DNS problem can make a website fail to load.

definition: A number that identifies a device or server on a network.
example: Only allow connections from this IP address.

definition: Internet Protocol. The basic rules for addressing and sending data across a network.
example: Each device on the network gets an IP address.

definition: Transmission Control Protocol. A reliable way of sending data that checks it arrives complete and in order.
example: Web pages are usually sent over TCP.

definition: HyperText Transfer Protocol. The set of rules browsers and servers use to exchange web pages and data.
example: The browser sent an HTTP request to the server.

definition: HTTP Secure. The same as HTTP, but the data is encrypted so others cannot read it.
example: Always log in on pages that use HTTPS.

definition: The delay between sending a request and getting a response.
example: High latency makes video calls lag.

definition: The maximum amount of data a connection can carry at one time.
example: Large downloads use a lot of bandwidth.

definition: A security tool that blocks or allows network traffic based on rules.
example: The firewall blocks connections from unknown addresses.

definition: A middle server that passes requests between you and the internet on your behalf.
example: Traffic goes through a proxy before reaching the website.

definition: A system that spreads incoming traffic across several servers so none gets overloaded.
example: The load balancer sends each visitor to a free server.

definition: A smaller section of a larger network.
example: Put the database in a separate subnet.

definition: Virtual Private Network. A secure, private tunnel for your internet traffic.
example: Connect to the VPN to reach the office network.

definition: A numbered entry point on a device where a specific service listens for connections.
example: Web servers usually listen on port 443.

definition: A device or server that connects one network to another.
example: The gateway links the office network to the internet.

definition: A small piece of data sent across a network.
example: Lost packets cause choppy video.

definition: Network traffic coming into a system.
example: Limit ingress to trusted addresses.

definition: Network traffic going out of a system.
example: You are billed for data egress.

definition: An error that happens when a response takes too long to arrive.
example: The request ended with a timeout.

definition: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures. A public ID number for a known security flaw.
example: The advisory lists the CVE so you can look up the flaw.

definition: Multi-Factor Authentication. Logging in with two or more proofs of identity, such as a password and a phone code.
example: Turn on MFA to protect your account.

definition: Scrambling data so only people with the right key can read it.
example: Encryption protects your files if a laptop is stolen.

definition: A trick where attackers pretend to be someone trustworthy to steal passwords or money.
example: The email was a phishing attempt.

definition: Harmful software made to damage systems or steal data.
example: The attachment contained malware.

definition: Malware that locks your files and demands payment to unlock them.
example: Ransomware locked every file on the server.

definition: A weakness in software or a system that attackers could use.
example: The vulnerability lets attackers read private data.

definition: A method or tool that takes advantage of a vulnerability.
example: Attackers released an exploit for the flaw.

definition: A software update that fixes a bug or security problem.
example: Install the patch as soon as possible.

definition: The steps taken to fix a problem or remove a threat.
example: Remediation includes updating the software.

definition: The login details that prove who you are, such as a username and password or a key.
example: Change your credentials after the breach.

definition: When an attacker can run any commands they choose on someone else's system.
example: The flaw allows arbitrary code execution on the server.

definition: Checking that you are who you say you are, usually by a password or code.
example: Authentication failed because the password was wrong.

definition: Deciding what a verified user is allowed to do or see.
example: Authorization decides whether you can open the admin page.

definition: A secret code sent with a request that proves you have permission. Whoever holds it can use it.
example: Send a valid bearer token with each request.

definition: A small secret code that proves you are logged in or allowed to use a service.
example: The token expires after one hour.

definition: A security flaw that attackers know about before the maker has released a fix.
example: The attack used a zero-day in the browser.

definition: Transport Layer Security. The technology that encrypts data traveling between your device and a website.
example: TLS keeps your password private on the way to the server.

definition: Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery. Automatic steps that test and release new code.
example: Our CI/CD pipeline deploys every change that passes the tests.

definition: A lightweight package that holds an app and everything it needs to run, so it works the same everywhere.
example: We run each service in its own container.

definition: A popular tool for building and running containers.
example: Build the Docker image and start it.

definition: A system that automatically starts, stops and manages many containers across many servers.
example: Kubernetes restarts the app if it crashes.

definition: Automatically adding or removing servers as demand goes up or down.
example: Autoscaling added servers during the sale.

definition: Pay-as-you-go pricing with no long-term commitment.
example: On-demand servers cost more per hour than reserved ones.

definition: Servers you commit to using for a long period, usually 1 to 3 years, in return for a lower price.
example: Reserved capacity lowers the monthly bill.

definition: Set up and reserved ahead of time for your use.
example: The database has 500 GB of provisioned storage.

definition: One virtual server running in the cloud.
example: Stop the instance to save money.

definition: Infrastructure as Code. Setting up servers and networks by writing files instead of clicking in a console.
example: We manage our cloud setup with IaC.

definition: The act of releasing a new version of software so people can use it.
example: The deployment finished at noon.

definition: Going back to the previous working version after a bad update.
example: We did a rollback after the release broke login.

definition: An app built from many small, separate services that work together.
example: Billing and search run as separate microservices.

definition: A way to run code where the cloud provider manages the servers for you and you pay only when the code runs.
example: The function runs serverless and costs nothing when idle.

definition: Input/Output Operations Per Second. How many reads and writes a storage disk can handle each second.
example: A database needs high IOPS to respond quickly.

definition: Cloud disk space that acts like a hard drive attached to a server.
example: Attach block storage to the instance.

definition: Service Level Agreement. A promise from a provider about how reliable the service will be.
example: The SLA guarantees 99.9% uptime.

definition: The share of time a service is working and available.
example: The site had 99.9% uptime last month.

definition: Structured Query Language. The standard language for asking a database to store or find data.
example: Write a SQL query to list all customers.

definition: Databases that store data in flexible formats instead of fixed tables.
example: We use a NoSQL database for user profiles.

definition: A question or request sent to a database.
example: The query returns all orders from today.

definition: A shortcut that helps a database find data faster, like the index of a book.
example: Add an index to speed up searches by email.

definition: The plan that describes how a database is organized: its tables, fields and types.
example: Changing the schema adds a new column.

definition: A unique value that identifies each row in a table.
example: The customer ID is the primary key.

definition: A field that links a row to a row in another table.
example: Each order has a foreign key pointing to a customer.

definition: A group of database changes that either all succeed or all fail together.
example: The transfer is one transaction, so money never disappears.

definition: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability. Four guarantees that keep database changes reliable.
example: ACID databases protect your data during crashes.

definition: Keeping copies of the same data on several servers.
example: Replication keeps a backup copy ready if one server fails.

definition: When two operations each wait for the other to finish, so neither can continue.
example: A deadlock stopped both updates.

definition: A planned change to a database's structure or a move of data to a new place.
example: Run the migration before starting the new version.

definition: Object-Relational Mapper. A tool that lets developers work with database tables using regular code.
example: The ORM turns code objects into database rows.

definition: Bad Request. The server could not understand the request because it was malformed.
example: HTTP 400 means something in the request was wrong.

definition: Unauthorized. You are not logged in or your login details are missing or invalid.
example: HTTP 401 appears when the token is missing.

definition: You are not logged in or your login details are missing or invalid.
example: The API returned 401 Unauthorized.

definition: Forbidden. The server knows who you are but you are not allowed to access this.
example: HTTP 403 means your account lacks permission.

definition: Not Found. The page or resource you asked for does not exist at that address.
example: HTTP 404 appears when a link is broken.

definition: The page or resource you asked for does not exist at that address.
example: The browser showed 404 Not Found.

definition: Too Many Requests. You sent too many requests in a short time and the server is asking you to slow down.
example: HTTP 429 means you hit the rate limit.

definition: You sent too many requests in a short time and the server is asking you to slow down.
example: The API returned 429 Too Many Requests.

definition: Internal Server Error. Something went wrong on the server's side.
example: HTTP 500 is a problem with the server, not with you.

definition: Something went wrong on the server's side.
example: The site showed 500 Internal Server Error.

definition: Bad Gateway. A server in the middle got an invalid answer from the server behind it.
example: HTTP 502 often means the app server is down.

definition: Service Unavailable. The server is overloaded or down for maintenance.
example: HTTP 503 usually clears up after a few minutes.

definition: Gateway Timeout. A server in the middle waited too long for an answer from the server behind it.
example: HTTP 504 means the app took too long to respond.

definition: The browser reached the server but it refused the connection, often because nothing is listening there.
example: ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED appears when the server is not running.

definition: The connection was refused, usually because the service is not running or the port is wrong.
example: ECONNREFUSED means nothing answered on that port.

definition: The connection attempt took too long and was cancelled.
example: ETIMEDOUT can happen when a firewall blocks the request.

definition: No such file or folder. The program looked for a file that does not exist.
example: ENOENT means the path is wrong.
